data.pattern_summary: Traverse tree structures by visiting nodes recursively along each branch, making it ideal for problems requiring structural modifications at every level.

pattern_options.name: Recursive Depth-First Search
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We visit every node and apply an operation to its children, which naturally fits a recursive tree traversal.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers are used for linear structures like arrays or strings, not hierarchical tree structures.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. We do not need to store and retrieve values by keys; we need to visit every node in the tree.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. There are no overlapping subproblems or optimal substructure decisions to cache here.

signals.hint: Signals that an operation must be applied uniformly to every node.

data.brute_force_idea: The provided solution directly uses a recursive function to swap the left and right pointers of each node as it visits them.
data.brute_force_why: Every node in the tree is visited exactly once.
data.bottleneck: The straightforward recursive approach is already optimal because every node must be visited at least once to have its children swapped.
bottleneck_hints: Consider whether you can solve this problem without visiting every single node.
Think about what happens if you skip even one node in the tree.
Since every node must be touched, an O(n) traversal is the theoretical limit.

data.overview: The algorithm uses a recursive Depth-First Search to invert a binary tree by swapping the left and right children of every node. It visits the root, recursively inverts its subtrees, and exchanges their references.
data.intuition: Imagine looking at a binary tree in a mirror; every left child becomes a right child and vice versa, which we can achieve by swapping subtrees from the bottom up.

data.insight: The brute-force solution wastes time converting the tree into a list and back, visiting nodes repeatedly. The optimized solution visits each node exactly once by performing the swap recursively during a standard depth-first traversal. By operating directly on the tree pointers, it eliminates redundant data structure conversions entirely.

derivation.note: Checks if the current node is null for every node plus base case leaves.
Recursively calls invertTree on the left child for every node.
Recursively calls invertTree on the right child for every node.
Assigns the inverted right child to the left pointer for every node.
Assigns the inverted left child to the right pointer for every node.

data.time_summary: Every node in the tree is visited a constant number of times. Summing the steps across all lines yields a linear total step count proportional to n, matching O(n).
data.space_summary: The call stack grows proportionally to the height of the tree, h, leading to O(h) extra space. In the worst-case skewed tree this is O(n), and in a balanced tree it is O(log n).
data.takeaway: When modifying trees, process subtrees recursively in place rather than serializing data structures.
mistakes: Serializing trees into lists when an in-place traversal is sufficient.
Forgetting to handle the base case where the node is null.
Swapping pointers without capturing the return values of recursive calls, leading to lost subtrees.
